newsitem.title: CHINA: Details stall food aid talks between rival Koreas.
newsitem.headline: Details stall food aid talks between rival Koreas.

text.p: Food aid talks between cold-war rivals Seoul and Pyongyang stalled on Saturday over the details of how to ship thousands of tonnes of grain from South Korea to help avert famine in the communist North, Seoul officials said.

Despite reaching basic agreement on Friday, talks in Beijing between negotiators from the Red Cross societies of the two Koreas had failed to resolve remaining differences, said Chang Moon-ik, spokesman of the South Korean embassy in China.
"Some parts of the agenda have not been agreed so one delegate of each side will meet again and will (try to) compromise," Chang told reporters after the morning talks.

The North-South negotiations would restart at 4.00 p.m. (0800 GMT) on Saturday, but practical difficulties meant it was unlikely an accord on the 40,000 tonnes of food aid promised by Seoul would be reached before the end of the day, he said.
"If the compromise is finished smoothly... then we'll sign," he said. "It may be impossible today."

Capitalist Seoul and communist Pyongyang have been technically at war since the 1950-53 Korean civil war ended only in a truce, and decades of mutual mistrust have made even basic food aid a delicate diplomatic affair.

Inter-Korean Red Cross talks earlier this month in Beijing failed after Seoul declined to say exactly how much aid it would supply to its Stalinist hermit neighbour, which aid workers say is facing widespread famine.

South Korea later promised to ship $8.0 million worth of corn, flour, powdered milk and instant noodles to the North by the end of July but details of how to transport, package and distribute the aid remained unresolved.

Lee Byung-woong, secretary general of the South Korean Red Cross delegation, had been pushing northern counterparts to accept direct transport through the town of Panmunjom on the highly militarised border between the two Koreas, Chang said.

North Korea, which takes self-reliance as its guiding ideology, has sought to limit any direct contact involved in taking southern grain, while Seoul wants to maximise exchanges and to make sure its aid is clearly labelled as such.

While the 40,000 tonnes of aid promised by Seoul is dwarfed by aid pledged by other donors -- the European Commission said on Friday it was sending 155,000 tonnes of food -- it could lead to further shipments from the prosperous South.
George Weber, Secretary General of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), said on Thursday he hoped the two sides would make progress.
While ethnic Korean residents in China who have visited the North have reported widespread starvation there, Weber said Pyongyang remained in a "pre-famine situation".

The situation in the isolated north Asian nation, which has seen a long-term economic decline compounded by two years of disastrous flooding, had become highly unstable, the European Commission's top envoy to Seoul said on Saturday.
"The situation is very explosive," Tue Rohrsted told a news conference. "Nobody knows whether it will explode or implode."
